Recent work supports separating order sensitivity from personalization and representation geometry. [Liu et al., RecSys 2025](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748042) show that arbitrary history shuffling confounds user behavior with item availability; constrained shuffling preserves items’ first-appearance boundaries. [Petrov et al., RecSys 2026](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling) find pairwise history models outperform Transformer reproductions on four of five benchmarks: strong ranking alone does not establish higher-order context use. [Zeng et al., ICLR 2025](https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2025/hash/2d2f85c0f93e69cf71f58eebaebb5e8d-Abstract-Conference.html) identify representation collapse and preference-changing augmentations as distinct concerns, motivating complementary behavioral probes.

Suggested diagnostic synthesis, rather than an established protocol: probe one frozen BERT4Rec using training-history prefixes, appended MASK, final nonpadding readout, and identical candidate sets across each paired comparison. Compare recent versus older deletion with equal deletion counts; permute older context while preserving the latest item, then separately perturb recent order; substitute another user’s history matched by length and item-frequency profile. Report paired target-rank changes, top-10 overlap, candidate-score correlation, representation cosine distance, and norm changes within length/frequency strata. Use identity perturbations in evaluation mode to establish numerical stability, repeated perturbation draws to quantify sampling variation, and user-level bootstrap intervals. Keep effective rank as complementary geometry evidence. Sensitivity demonstrates dependence on the altered input; it does not establish useful personalization, causal intent, or improvement in host validation HR@10. These controls require no additional fitted predictor or score fusion.
